title: Bounded-above finite-projective sheaf Hom model
statement:
Let $(\mathcal C,\mathcal O)$ be a ringed site, where $\mathcal C$ is a site and $\mathcal O$ a sheaf of commutative rings, small in the universe of its module sheaves [def-weil-pbc-sites-and-cohomology, def-weil-size-convention, def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. Let $P^\bullet,N^\bullet$ be cochain complexes of $\mathcal O$-modules [def-pc-cochain-complex-modules]. Suppose there are integers $a,b$ such that $P^i=0$ for $i>b$ and $N^j=0$ for $j<a$, and for each $i$ the sheaf $P^i$ is isomorphic to a direct summand of $\mathcal O^{\oplus r_i}$ for a finite nonnegative integer $r_i$. Then, in the derived category [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], $R\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O}(QP,QN)$ [def-pur-derived-internal-hom] is canonically represented by $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(P,N)$ [def-pur-hom-complex]. Its degree-$n$ term is
$$\mathcal Hom^n(P,N)=\bigoplus_{a-n\leq i\leq b}\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O}(P^i,N^{i+n}),$$
and its differential on a degree-$n$ family $f$ is $d_Nf-(-1)^nf d_P$. Here $Q$ denotes localization at quasi-isomorphisms, and $\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O}$ is the sheaf Hom [def-pur-sheaf-hom].

proof.text: The category $\Mod(\mathcal O)$ is Grothendieck by [prop-pur-kinjective-resolutions-exist], hence has enough injectives by [lem-sp-grothendieck-enough-injectives]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-dplus-injective-representative] to $QN$, whose cohomology vanishes below $a$, to obtain a complex $I$ of injectives with $I^j=0$ for $j<a$, an isomorphism $QN\cong QI$, and K-injectivity of $I$. By [lem-weil-pbc-kinjective-hom-derived] this isomorphism lifts to a homotopy class represented by a chain map $\alpha:N\to I$. Since cohomology factors through localization [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], every $H^j(\alpha)$ is an isomorphism, so $\alpha$ is a quasi-isomorphism. This supplies an actual bounded-below replacement map, not just an isomorphism of derived objects.

For a finite free sheaf $F=\mathcal O^{\oplus r}$, evaluation on its basis on every slice gives $\mathcal Hom(F,M)\cong M^{\oplus r}$ naturally in $M$, by [def-pur-sheaf-hom]. Thus $\mathcal Hom(F,\alpha)$ is a quasi-isomorphism: kernels, images and their quotients in a finite biproduct are the finite biproducts of the respective kernels, images and quotients. Choose splitting maps exhibiting $P^i$ as a summand of such an $F$, so $F\cong P^i\oplus T$. The Hom complexes and their cohomology split into the two corresponding summands. The inverse of the cohomology map for $F$ commutes with the splitting idempotent (the map itself commutes with it), and therefore restricts to an inverse on the $P^i$ summand. Consequently $\mathcal Hom(P^i,\alpha)$ is a quasi-isomorphism for every $i$. This is internal sheaf Hom, and makes no assertion that $P^i$ is projective for global Hom.

Put $c=a-b$. For $M=N$ or $I$ form the first-quadrant double complex $D_M^{u,v}=\mathcal Hom(P^{b-u},M^{a+v})$ for $u,v\geq0$, and zero elsewhere [def-sp-double-complex-total]. Its horizontal differential is precomposition by $d_P^{b-u-1}$ and its vertical differential is postcomposition by $d_M^{a+v}$; they commute and both square to zero. In translated total degree $n=u+v+c$ the Hom differential [def-pur-hom-complex] is postcomposition by $d_M$ plus $(-1)^{n+1}$ times precomposition by $d_P$. The standard total differential is horizontal plus $(-1)^u$ vertical. Multiplication on the $(u,v)$ summand by $s(u,v)=(-1)^{uv+u(u-1)/2+u(c+1)}$ identifies this standard total, with degrees translated by $c$, with the Hom complex: $s(u,v+1)=(-1)^u s(u,v)$ verifies the vertical term and $s(u+1,v)=(-1)^{u+v+c+1}s(u,v)$ verifies the horizontal term. All signs are units even in characteristic two. Translation here leaves the differential unchanged and merely renames degree $t$ as $t+c$, so it also merely renames the cohomology degree.

Postcomposition with $\alpha$ gives a double-complex map $D_N\to D_I$ commuting with both differentials. For each fixed $u$, the vertical complex is $\mathcal Hom(P^{b-u},M^{a+\bullet})$, and the induced map is a quasi-isomorphism by step 2. Apply [lem-sc-first-quadrant-total-column-comparison] in the abelian category $\Mod(\mathcal O)$ [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. Its first-quadrant and column hypotheses are exactly those just checked. Hence the total map is a quasi-isomorphism. The summand signs in step 3 depend only on $u,v,a,b$, so commute with postcomposition by $\alpha$ and identify this total map with $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(P,\alpha)$. Translating degrees preserves kernels and images. Therefore $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(P,N)\to\mathcal Hom^\bullet(P,I)$ is a quasi-isomorphism. The arrow is in this direction, contrary to the reversed arrow in one sentence of the source proof.

By [def-pur-derived-internal-hom], the Hom complex into a K-injective replacement computes $R\mathcal Hom(QP,QN)$. Thus the quasi-isomorphism in step 4 gives the claimed derived isomorphism. Its canonicity can also be checked directly: for two K-injective replacements $\alpha:N\to I$, $\alpha':N\to J$, [lem-weil-pbc-kinjective-hom-derived] lifts the derived morphism $Q\alpha'\,(Q\alpha)^{-1}:QI\to QJ$ to a chain map $h:I\to J$, unique up to homotopy. Injectivity of the same localization bijection with source $N$ and target $J$ implies that $h\alpha$ is homotopic to $\alpha'$. Applying internal Hom from $P$ preserves target homotopies: for a homotopy $k$ the degree-minus-one map on Hom families is $f\mapsto kf$, and expansion of the Hom differential gives $d(kf)+k(df)=(d_Jk+kd_I)f$. Therefore the two comparison diagrams commute in the derived category [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. The comparison of replacements is a quasi-isomorphism since its localization is $Q\alpha'\,(Q\alpha)^{-1}$; [lem-pur-rhom-well-defined] gives the quasi-isomorphism on internal Hom. This identifies the isomorphism with the resolution-independent canonical one, rather than a chosen unrelated isomorphism.

Finally the degree-$n$ product of [def-pur-hom-complex] has a nonzero factor only when $i\leq b$ and $i+n\geq a$, equivalently $a-n\leq i\leq b$. Removing zero factors leaves a finite product, canonically the finite biproduct, giving the displayed direct sum. If the interval is empty it is the zero object. The differential is exactly $d_Nf-(-1)^nf d_P$ from that definition; no change of signs is made in the asserted model.
